fields.title: A case study without numbers is just a testimonial
fields.keyTakeaway: A case study answers three questions: what was happening, what was done, and what changed — and the third one must be a number. Without a number, you just get a nice story that proves nothing.
fields.checkQuestion: "The client really liked the service, work became more convenient." What is wrong here?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **what results should we tell consumers about?** A case study is proof from the lesson on messaging, just expanded.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer the question.** An "Our Clients" page appears with logos and quotes like "convenient and fast". The reader cannot apply this to themselves because they do not know if the client was like them.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Three parts, and the third one decides
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Situation** — who the client is and what was broken. Detailed enough for the reader to recognize themselves.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **What was done** — not a feature list, but how the process changed.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Result** — a number: it was this much, it became this much, in this timeframe.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Caveat** — what else had an effect. An honest case study is stronger than an ideal one: people believe it.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Situation: a manufacturing company of 12 people, 60 acceptance certificates a month, a certificate took an average of 4 days by email, delaying the month-end closing as a result.

What was done: moved signing with counterparties to the browser, starting with the eight most frequent counterparties.

Result: signing time of 6 hours instead of 4 days for these eight; month-end closing stopped slipping. Measured over two months.

Caveat: signing time did not change for the remaining counterparties — they are not connected yet.

The caveat did not weaken the case study: it was what turned it from an ad into a realistic description of what to expect.
fields.blocks/4/text: A case study convinces people in similar situations: a 12-person manufacturing company says nothing to a 400-employee chain. That is why you need several case studies, one per segment, rather than a single most attractive one. And client approval takes weeks — factor this into your timelines.
